text: The de-Broglie wavelength of an electron is the same as that of a photon. If velocity of electron is $25%$ of the velocity of light, then the ratio of K.E. of electron and K.E. of photon will be:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
We know that the de-Broglie wavelength $λ$ of a particle is given by:

$λ=\frac{h}{p}$

where:

$h$ is Planck's constant,

$p$ is the momentum of the particle.

For a photon (which has zero rest mass), its energy $E$ and momentum $p$ are related by the equation:

$E=cp$

and its de-Broglie wavelength $λ$ is given by:

$λ=\frac{hc}{E}$

Now, since the photon and electron are said to have the same de-Broglie wavelength:

$λ_{electron}=λ_{photon}$

$\frac{h}{p_{electron}}=\frac{hc}{E_{photon}}$

For the electron, its momentum $p_{electron}$ is given by:

$p_{electron}=m_{e}v_{electron}$

where:

$m_{e}$ is the electron's rest mass,

$v_{electron}$ is the electron's velocity.

The kinetic energy $K.E.$ of the electron is:

$K.E._{electron}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}v_{electron}^{2}$

The question states that $v_{electron}$ is $25%$ ($0.25c$) of the speed of light $c$. So we write:

$v_{electron}=0.25c$

Plugging this into the kinetic energy formula, we get:

$K.E._{electron}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}(0.25c)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}\times \frac{1}{16}c^{2}$

$K.E._{electron}=\frac{1}{32}m_{e}c^{2}$

For a photon, $p_{photon}=\frac{E_{photon}}{c}$ and hence its kinetic energy (which, for a photon, is simply its energy) is:

$K.E._{photon}=E_{photon}=cp_{photon}$

Now, comparing the kinetic energies:

$\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{photon}}=\frac{\frac{1}{32}m_{e}c^{2}}{cp_{photon}}$

Since $p_{electron}=p_{photon}$ (from the de-Broglie relation), we can replace $p_{photon}$ with $p_{electron}$ which is $m_{e}v_{electron}$:

$\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{photon}}=\frac{\frac{1}{32}m_{e}c^{2}}{m_{e}v_{electron}c}$

$\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{photon}}=\frac{\frac{1}{32}c}{0.25c}$

$\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{photon}}=\frac{1}{32}\times \frac{1}{0.25}$

$\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{photon}}=\frac{1}{32}\times 4$

$\frac{K.E._{electron}}{K.E._{photon}}=\frac{1}{8}$

So the correct answer is Option C $\frac{1}{8}$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: The deflection in moving coil galvanometer falls from 25 divisions to 5 divisions when a shunt of $24\Omega$ is applied. The resistance of galvanometer coil will be :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let $x$ be the current per division. The current $I$ in the circuit is the same before and after the shunt is connected. Without the shunt the whole current passes through the galvanometer, which shows 25 divisions:

$I=25x$

With the $24\Omega$ shunt the galvanometer shows 5 divisions, so it carries $I_{g}=5x$ and the shunt carries $I-I_{g}=20x$.


[IMG]

The galvanometer and the shunt are in parallel, so the potential differences across them are equal:

$I_{g}G=(I-I_{g})S\Rightarrow 5x\times G=20x\times 24$

$G=4\times 24=96\Omega$

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text: At what distance above and below the surface of the earth a body will have same weight. (take radius of earth as $R$.)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
At height $h$ above the surface, $g_{h}=\dfrac{gR^{2}}{(R+h)^{2}}$; at depth $h$ below the surface of a uniform earth, $g_{d}=g\left (1-\dfrac{h}{R}\right )$. Both expressions are exact, so no $h\ll R$ approximation is used.


[IMG]

Equal weight requires $g_{h}=g_{d}$. With $x=\dfrac{h}{R}$:

$\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}=1-x\Rightarrow (1-x)(1+x)^{2}=1$

Expanding, $(1-x^{2})(1+x)=1+x-x^{2}-x^{3}=1$, so

$x\left (x^{2}+x-1\right )=0$

For $x\neq 0$, the positive root of $x^{2}+x-1=0$ is

$x=\frac{-1+\sqrt{1+4}}{2}=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}\approx 0.62$

Since $x<1$, the lower point lies inside the earth, and

$h=\frac{\sqrt{5}R-R}{2}$

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text: A galvanometer having coil resistance $10\Omega$ shows a full scale deflection for a current of $3\mathrm{mA}$. For it to measure a current of $8\mathrm{A}$, the value of the shunt should be:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
[IMG]

To determine the value of the shunt resistor required to convert the galvanometer into an ammeter capable of measuring a current of $8\mathrm{A}$, we need to use the concept of shunting where the additional resistor (shunt) is placed in parallel with the galvanometer.

The formula for calculating the value of the shunt resistor $R_{s}$ is given by:

$R_{s}=\frac{R_{g}\cdot I_{g}}{I-I_{g}}$

Where:

$R_{g}$ = resistance of the galvanometer = $10\Omega$

$I_{g}$ = full-scale deflection current of the galvanometer = $3\mathrm{mA}$ = $0.003\mathrm{A}$

$I$ = total current to be measured = $8\mathrm{A}$

Substituting these values into the formula:

$R_{s}=\frac{10\Omega \cdot 0.003\mathrm{A}}{8\mathrm{A}-0.003\mathrm{A}}$

Perform the calculations:

$R_{s}=\frac{0.03\Omega \cdot \mathrm{A}}{7.997\mathrm{A}}$

$R_{s}\approx 3.75\times 10^{-3}\Omega$

Thus, the value of the shunt resistor should be:

Option A: $3.75\times 10^{-3}\Omega$

text: Two charges of $5Q$ and $-2Q$ are situated at the points $(3a,0)$ and $(-5a,0)$ respectively. The electric flux through a sphere of radius '$4a$' having center at origin is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The electric flux through any closed surface is given by Gauss's law, which can be stated as:

$\Phi =\frac{Q_{\text{enc}}}{ε_{0}}$

where:

    $\Phi$ = electric flux
    $Q_{\text{enc}}$ = total charge enclosed by the surface
    $ε_{0}$ = permittivity of free space (electric constant)

In this scenario, we have a sphere of radius $4a$ with its center at the origin and two charges, $5Q$ at point (3a, 0) and $-2Q$ at point (-5a, 0). Since the sphere's radius is $4a$, the charge $5Q$, which is located at (3a, 0), lies inside the sphere, whereas the charge $-2Q$, located at (-5a, 0), lies outside the sphere. Gauss's law only considers charges that are enclosed within the surface.

Thus, the charge $-2Q$ has no impact on the electric flux through the sphere because it is not enclosed by the sphere. Only the charge $5Q$ contributes to the electric flux inside the sphere.

The electric flux through the sphere is therefore given simply by the enclosed charge:

$\Phi =\frac{5Q}{ε_{0}}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: A biconvex lens of refractive index 1.5 has a focal length of $20\mathrm{cm}$ in air. Its focal length when immersed in a liquid of refractive index 1.6 will be:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In air, the lens maker's formula with $μ_{g}=1.5$ and $f_{a}=20\text{cm}$ gives the curvature factor of the lens:

$\frac{1}{f_{a}}=(μ_{g}-1)\left (\frac{1}{R_{1}}-\frac{1}{R_{2}}\right )\Rightarrow \left (\frac{1}{R_{1}}-\frac{1}{R_{2}}\right )=\frac{1}{0.5\times 20}=\frac{1}{10}\text{cm}^{-1}$

In the liquid ($μ_{l}=1.6$), the refractive index of glass relative to the surrounding medium is $\dfrac{μ_{g}}{μ_{l}}$:

$\frac{1}{f_{l}}=\left (\frac{μ_{g}}{μ_{l}}-1\right )\left (\frac{1}{R_{1}}-\frac{1}{R_{2}}\right )=\left (\frac{1.5}{1.6}-1\right )\times \frac{1}{10}=-\frac{1}{16}\times \frac{1}{10}=-\frac{1}{160}\text{cm}^{-1}$

$f_{l}=-160\text{cm}$

The negative sign shows that the biconvex lens behaves as a diverging lens in the liquid, which is optically denser than the glass.

Hence, the correct option is (D).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: A body starts moving from rest with constant acceleration covers displacement $S_{1}$ in first $(p-1)$ seconds and $\mathrm{S}_{2}$ in first $p$ seconds. The displacement $\mathrm{S}_{1}+\mathrm{S}_{2}$ will be made in time :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let's denote the constant acceleration with which the body moves as $a$. We know that the displacement $S$ covered by a body starting from rest under a constant acceleration $a$ in time $t$ is given by the equation of motion: $S=\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$.

Considering the displacement $\mathrm{S}_{1}$ in first $(p-1)$ seconds, we apply the equation of motion:

$\mathrm{S}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}a(p-1)^{2}$

Similarly, for the displacement $\mathrm{S}_{2}$ in first $p$ seconds:

$\mathrm{S}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}ap^{2}$

To find out the total time it will take to cover the displacement $\mathrm{S}_{1}+\mathrm{S}_{2}$, we first find the sum of these two displacements:

$\mathrm{S}_{1}+\mathrm{S}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}a(p-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}ap^{2}$

Let's simplify this:

$\mathrm{S}_{1}+\mathrm{S}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}a\left ((p-1)^{2}+p^{2}\right )$
$\mathrm{S}_{1}+\mathrm{S}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}a\left (p^{2}-2p+1+p^{2}\right )$
$\mathrm{S}_{1}+\mathrm{S}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}a\left (2p^{2}-2p+1\right )$
$\mathrm{S}_{1}+\mathrm{S}_{2}=a\left (\frac{2p^{2}-2p+1}{2}\right )$

If we consider the total displacement $\mathrm{S}_{1}+\mathrm{S}_{2}$ is to be covered in a time $t$ seconds from rest, we should set this equal to the equation of motion:

$\mathrm{S}_{1}+\mathrm{S}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$

Equating the two equations:

$a\left (\frac{2p^{2}-2p+1}{2}\right )=\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$

Since $a\neq 0$, we can simplify by dividing both sides by $\frac{1}{2}a$:

$\frac{2p^{2}-2p+1}{2}=\frac{t^{2}}{2}$
$2p^{2}-2p+1=t^{2}$

To find $t$, we take the square root of both sides:

$t=\sqrt{2p^{2}-2p+1}$

Therefore, the time taken to cover the displacement $\mathrm{S}_{1}+\mathrm{S}_{2}$ will be:

$t=\sqrt{(2p^{2}-2p+1)}s$

Hence, the correct option would be:

Option D: $\sqrt{(2p^{2}-2p+1)}s$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: The electric current through a wire varies with time as $I=I_{0}+βt$, where $I_{0}=20\mathrm{A}$ and $β=3\mathrm{A}/\mathrm{s}$. The amount of electric charge crossed through a section of the wire in $20\mathrm{s}$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To calculate the amount of electric charge $Q$ that crosses through a section of the wire over a period of $20$ seconds, given the current varies with time as $I=I_{0}+βt$, where $I_{0}=20$ A (initial current) and $β=3$ A/s (rate of change of current with time), we use the concept of integration from calculus because the current is not constant but changes linearly with time.

The electric charge $Q$ is the integral of current $I$ over the time interval from $0$ to $20$ seconds. The formula for $Q$ is given by:

$Q=\int\limits _{0}^{T}I(t)dt$

Where $I(t)=I_{0}+βt$ and $T=20$ s. Substituting the given values:

$Q=\int\limits _{0}^{20}(20+3t)dt$

This integral can be solved in two parts:

1. The integral of the constant term $20$:

$\int 20dt=20t$

2. The integral of the linear term $3t$:

$\int 3tdt=\frac{3}{2}t^{2}$

Thus, combining these and evaluating from $0$ to $20$ seconds:

$Q=\left [20t+\frac{3}{2}t^{2}\right ]_{0}^{20}$

$Q=\left [20(20)+\frac{3}{2}(20)^{2}\right ]-\left [20(0)+\frac{3}{2}(0)^{2}\right ]$

$Q=400+600=1000$ C

Therefore, the amount of electric charge that crosses through a section of the wire in $20$ seconds is $1000$ C.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: The potential energy function (in $J$ ) of a particle in a region of space is given as $U=\left (2x^{2}+3y^{3}+2z\right )$. Here $x,y$ and $z$ are in meter. The magnitude of $x$-component of force (in $N$ ) acting on the particle at point $P(1,2,3)\mathrm{m}$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The force acting on a particle can be determined from the potential energy function by using the negative gradient. In three-dimensional space, the force vector F is related to the potential energy function $U$ by:

$𝐅=-\nabla U$

where $\nabla U$ (the gradient of $U$) is a vector with components given by the partial derivatives of $U$ with respect to $x$, $y$, and $z$:

$\nabla U=\left (\frac{𝜕U}{𝜕x},\frac{𝜕U}{𝜕y},\frac{𝜕U}{𝜕z}\right )$

Given the potential energy function:

$U=2x^{2}+3y^{3}+2z$

Calculate the partial derivative of $U$ with respect to $x$ to find the $x$-component of the force:

Partial Derivative with respect to $x$:

$\frac{𝜕U}{𝜕x}=\frac{𝜕}{𝜕x}(2x^{2}+3y^{3}+2z)=4x$

Calculate the $x$-component of the force:

Since $F_{x}=-\frac{𝜕U}{𝜕x}$, the $x$-component of the force is:

$F_{x}=-4x$

Evaluate at point $P(1,2,3)$:

Substitute $x=1$ into the expression for $F_{x}$:

$F_{x}=-4(1)=-4$

The magnitude of the $x$-component of the force is:

$|F_{x}|=4\text{N}$

text:
The explosive in a Hydrogen bomb is a mixture of ${}_{1}\mathrm{H}^{2},{}_{1}\mathrm{H}^{3}$ and ${}_{3}\mathrm{Li}^{6}$ in some condensed form. The chain reaction is given by

$\begin{array}{l} {}_{3}\mathrm{Li}^{6}+{}_{0}\mathrm{n}^{1}\to {}_{2}\mathrm{He}^{4}+{}_{1}\mathrm{H}^{3} \\ {}_{1}\mathrm{H}^{2}+{}_{1}\mathrm{H}^{3}\to {}_{2}\mathrm{He}^{4}+{}_{0}\mathrm{n}^{1} \end{array}$

During the explosion the energy released is approximately

[Given ; $\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{Li})=6.01690\mathrm{amu},\mathrm{M}\left ({}_{1}\mathrm{H}^{2}\right )=2.01471\mathrm{amu},\mathrm{M}\left ({}_{2}\mathrm{He}^{4}\right )=4.00388$ $\mathrm{amu}$, and $1\mathrm{amu}=931.5\mathrm{MeV}]$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\begin{array}{l} {}_{3}\mathrm{Li}^{6}+{}_{0}\mathrm{n}^{1}\to {}_{2}\mathrm{He}^{4}+{}_{1}\mathrm{H}^{3} \\ {}_{1}\mathrm{H}^{2}+{}_{1}\mathrm{H}^{3}\to {}_{2}\mathrm{He}^{4}+{}_{0}\mathrm{n}^{1} \\ {}_{3}\mathrm{Li}^{6}+{}_{1}\mathrm{H}^{2}\to 2\left ({}_{2}\mathrm{He}^{4}\right ) \\  \end{array}$

Energy released in process

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{Q}=\Delta \mathrm{mc}^{2} \\ \mathrm{Q}=\left [\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{Li})+\mathrm{M}\left (\mathrm{H}^{2}\right )-2\times \mathrm{M}\left ({}_{2}\mathrm{He}^{4}\right )\right ]\times 931.5\mathrm{MeV} \\ \mathrm{Q}=[6.01690+2.01471-2\times 4.00388]\times 931.5\mathrm{MeV} \\ \mathrm{Q}=22.216\mathrm{MeV} \\ \mathrm{Q}=22.22\mathrm{MeV} \end{array}$

text:
In a double slit experiment shown in figure, when light of wavelength $400\mathrm{nm}$ is used, dark fringe is observed at $P$. If $\mathrm{D}=0.2\mathrm{m}$, the minimum distance between the slits $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ is $_________$ $\mathrm{mm}$.


[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Path difference for minima at $\mathrm{P}$

$\begin{array}{l} 2\sqrt{\mathrm{D}^{2}+\mathrm{d}^{2}}-2\mathrm{D}=\dfrac{λ}{2} \\ \therefore \sqrt{\mathrm{D}^{2}+\mathrm{d}^{2}}-\mathrm{D}=\dfrac{λ}{4} \\ \therefore \sqrt{\mathrm{D}^{2}+\mathrm{d}^{2}}=\dfrac{λ}{4}+\mathrm{D} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{D}^{2}+\mathrm{d}^{2}=\mathrm{D}^{2}+\dfrac{λ^{2}}{16}+\dfrac{\mathrm{D}λ}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{d}^{2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{D}λ}{2}+\dfrac{λ^{2}}{16} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{d}^{2}=\dfrac{0.2\times 400\times 10^{-9}}{2}+\dfrac{4\times 10^{-14}}{4} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{d}^{2}\approx 400\times 10^{-10} \\ \therefore \mathrm{d}=20\times 10^{-5} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{d}=0.20\mathrm{mm} \end{array}$

text: A cylinder is rolling down on an inclined plane of inclination $60^{\circ }$. Its acceleration during rolling down will be $\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}m/s^{2}$, where $x=$ $________ ($use $\mathrm{g}=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$).
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine the acceleration of a cylinder rolling down an inclined plane without slipping, we can use Newton's second law and the concept of rolling motion. For an inclined plane at an angle $θ$, the component of gravitational acceleration along the plane is $g\sin θ$. However, because the cylinder is rolling and not sliding, not all of this component accelerates the center of mass; some of it goes into causing rotational acceleration about the center of mass.

For a rolling cylinder, the moment of inertia $I$ is $I=\frac{1}{2}mr^{2}$, where $m$ is the mass of the cylinder and $r$ is the radius. The condition for rolling without slipping is that the linear acceleration $a$ of the center of mass is equal to the radius $r$ times the angular acceleration $α$, i.e., $a=rα$.

To find the linear acceleration $a$, we use the torque $τ$ about the center of mass caused by the gravitational force down the incline. The torque due to gravity is $τ=mg\sin θ\cdot r$, and from Newton's second law for rotation, the angular acceleration is given by

$α=\frac{τ}{I}=\frac{mg\sin θ\cdot r}{\frac{1}{2}mr^{2}}=\frac{2g\sin θ}{r}$

Now using $a=rα$:

$a=r\left (\frac{2g\sin θ}{r}\right )=2g\sin θ$

But we must account for the fact that only a portion of the gravitational acceleration goes into translating the cylinder down the plane due to the rolling condition. This is where we apply the concept of the ``rolling factor'' for a cylinder, which is $\frac{2}{3}$ for a solid cylinder, meaning $\frac{2}{3}$ of the gravitational component is used for translation.

The acceleration of the center of mass for the cylinder is therefore:

$a=\frac{2}{3}g\sin θ$

Now we plug in the values of $θ=60^{\circ }$ (which has $\sin 60^{\circ }=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$) and $g=10m/s^{2}$:

$a=\frac{2}{3}\cdot 10\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{10\sqrt{3}}{3}$

To match the given expression $\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}m/s^{2}$, let's manipulate our expression for $a$:

$a=\frac{10\sqrt{3}}{3}=\frac{10\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{10\cdot 3}{3\cdot \sqrt{3}}=\frac{10}{\sqrt{3}}m/s^{2}$

Hence, the value of $x$ is $10$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: An electron is moving under the influence of the electric field of a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet $\mathrm{S}$ having surface charge density $+σ$. The electron at $t=0$ is at a distance of $1\mathrm{m}$ from $S$ and has a speed of $1\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$. The maximum value of $σ$ if the electron strikes $S$ at $t=1\mathrm{s}$ is $α\left [\frac{m𝜖_{0}}{e}\right ]\frac{\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{m}^{2}}$, the value of $α$ is $___________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The field of the sheet is uniform, $E=\dfrac{σ}{2ε_{0}}$, directed away from the sheet, so the electron has a constant acceleration towards the sheet:

$a=\frac{eE}{m}=\frac{eσ}{2ε_{0}m}$

Let $x$ be the distance from the sheet ($x=1\text{m}$ at $t=0$) and $v_{⟂}$ the component of the initial velocity directed away from the sheet, with $-1\text{m s}^{-1}\leq v_{⟂}\leq 1\text{m s}^{-1}$. Then

$x=1+v_{⟂}t-\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$

The electron reaches the sheet ($x=0$) at $t=1\text{s}$:

$0=1+v_{⟂}-\frac{a}{2}\Rightarrow a=2(1+v_{⟂})$

So $a$, and hence $σ$, is largest when the electron initially moves directly away from the sheet, $v_{⟂}=1\text{m s}^{-1}$, giving $a=4\text{m s}^{-2}$; then $x=1+t-2t^{2}$ first becomes zero at $t=1\text{s}$.

$σ_{\max }=\frac{2ε_{0}ma}{e}=8\left [\frac{mε_{0}}{e}\right ]\text{C m}^{-2}$

Hence, the answer is 8.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: When a hydrogen atom going from $n=2$ to $n=1$ emits a photon, its recoil speed is $\frac{x}{5}\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$. Where $x=$ $________. ($Use, mass of hydrogen atom $=1.6\times 10^{-27}\mathrm{kg}$)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For hydrogen, $E_{2}=-3.4\text{eV}$ and $E_{1}=-13.6\text{eV}$.


[IMG]

The photon emitted in the $n=2\to n=1$ transition has energy

$E=E_{2}-E_{1}=10.2\text{eV}=10.2\times 1.6\times 10^{-19}\text{J}$

The atom was at rest, so by momentum conservation its recoil momentum equals the photon momentum $\dfrac{E}{c}$:

$mv=\dfrac{E}{c}\Rightarrow v=\dfrac{E}{mc}$

$v=\dfrac{10.2\times 1.6\times 10^{-19}}{1.6\times 10^{-27}\times 3\times 10^{8}}=3.4\text{m s}^{-1}$

Since $v=\dfrac{x}{5}$, $x=5\times 3.4=17$.

Hence, the answer is 17.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: A $16\Omega$ wire is bent to form a square loop. A $9\mathrm{V}$ battery with internal resistance $1\Omega$ is connected across one of its sides. If a $4μF$ capacitor is connected across one of its diagonals, the energy stored by the capacitor will be $\frac{x}{2}μJ$, where $x=$ $_________$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Each side of the square has resistance $\dfrac{16}{4}=4\Omega$. The battery is connected across one side, so that side ($4\Omega$) is in parallel with the other three sides in series ($12\Omega$):


[IMG]

$R_{\text{ext}}=\dfrac{4\times 12}{4+12}=3\Omega ,I=\dfrac{9}{3+1}=\dfrac{9}{4}\text{A}$

At steady state the capacitor draws no current, and the three-side path carries

$I_{1}=\dfrac{9}{4}\times \dfrac{4}{4+12}=\dfrac{9}{16}\text{A}$

Either diagonal joins two corners that are two sides apart along this path, so the capacitor voltage is

$V=I_{1}\times 8\Omega =\dfrac{9}{16}\times 8=\dfrac{9}{2}\text{V}$

$U=\dfrac{1}{2}CV^{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\times \left (\dfrac{9}{2}\right )^{2}μ\text{J}=\dfrac{81}{2}μ\text{J}$

Hence, the answer is 81.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: When the displacement of a simple harmonic oscillator is one third of its amplitude, the ratio of total energy to the kinetic energy is $\frac{x}{8}$, where $x=$ $_________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body: $\begin{array}{l} \text{Let total energy}=\mathrm{E}=\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{KA}^{2} \\ \mathrm{U}=\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{K}\left (\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{3}\right )^{2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{KA}^{2}}{2\times 9}=\dfrac{\mathrm{E}}{9} \\ \mathrm{KE}=\mathrm{E}-\dfrac{\mathrm{E}}{9}=\dfrac{8\mathrm{E}}{9} \\ \text{Ratio}\dfrac{\text{Total}}{\mathrm{KE}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{E}}{\frac{8\mathrm{E}}{9}}=\dfrac{9}{8} \\ \mathrm{x}=9 \end{array}$

text: A ball rolls off the top of a stairway with horizontal velocity $u$. The steps are $0.1\mathrm{m}$ high and $0.1\mathrm{m}$ wide. The minimum velocity $u$ with which that ball just hits the step 5 of the stairway will be $\sqrt{x}\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$ where $x=$ $__________$ [use $\mathrm{g}=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$ ].
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
[IMG]


The ball needs to just cross 4 steps to just hit $5^{\text{th}}$ step

Therefore, horizontal range $(R)=0.4\mathrm{m}$

$\mathrm{R}=\text{u.t}$

Similarly, in vertical direction

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{h}=\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{gt}^{2} \\ 0.4=\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{gt}^{2} \\ 0.4=\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{g}\left (\dfrac{0.4}{\mathrm{u}}\right )^{2} \\ \mathrm{u}^{2}=2 \\ \mathrm{u}=\sqrt{2}\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s} \end{array}$

Therefore, $\mathrm{x}=2$
